cards.title: Choose premiums that fit the buyer and the product
cards.summary: Use a product-related premium or discount that helps the buyer justify the purchase, rather than an unrelated giveaway that attracts low-intent responders.
cards.use_when: Designing a first-order bonus, email-capture incentive, wholesale promotion, or product-launch offer for an ecommerce store.
steps: Start with the buyer’s purchasing context. For a consumer order, offer a bonus that improves use of the purchased product: a guide, accessory, refill, sample, or complementary item. For wholesale or corporate buyers, favor a discount or a premium that creates value for their company rather than a personal-use gift.

Make the premium visibly connected to the product category. A skincare store might offer a regimen guide or travel-size complementary product; a specialty-food seller might offer a pairing guide or sample of a related flavor.

Use related premiums for lead capture as well as orders. A downloadable buying guide, product-specific checklist, or comparison guide gives a prospect a concrete reason to subscribe and is more likely to attract qualified shoppers than a generic prize.
If using an unrelated, high-value giveaway, treat it as a volume tactic and separately assess lead quality, subsequent purchase rate, and margin.
Show the premium clearly on the landing page, PDP, cart, or signup form so shoppers can understand what they receive and why it matters.
caveats: The source presents related premiums as personal experience rather than a universal rule; an unrelated giveaway can be appropriate when broad reach, not immediate qualification, is the objective.
Discounting can condition buyers to wait for promotions and reduce contribution margin.

cards.title: Use samples and evaluations to prove fit before purchase
cards.summary: Let shoppers test the product on their own need, material, or configuration when generic product claims cannot establish fit.
cards.use_when: Selling configurable, technical, high-consideration, or sensory products online where a shopper needs evidence before committing to a full purchase.
steps: Identify the uncertainty blocking the sale: material compatibility, sizing, output quality, taste, shade, texture, or configuration. Build the sample around resolving that specific uncertainty rather than sending a generic freebie.

Where feasible, let the customer submit the relevant input or specification. The source’s B2B illustrations include evaluating a customer water sample and running a customer-supplied material through equipment; an ecommerce equivalent could be a custom swatch, compatibility review, shade-match consultation, or configuration check.
Return a useful result that demonstrates the product’s capability: a sample, recommendation, proof, configured preview, or clear go/no-go assessment.

State the request requirements, fulfillment timeline, and any shipping terms before the shopper opts in. Capture only the information necessary to produce the evaluation and follow up when the result is ready.
Use the evaluation outcome to direct the shopper to the appropriate SKU, bundle, or replenishment plan instead of leaving them with an unstructured trial experience.
caveats: The source examples are primarily B2B; apply the underlying proof-of-fit structure rather than treating their outcomes as ecommerce evidence.
Samples and custom evaluations create fulfillment cost and operational complexity, so model eligibility, turnaround, and abuse controls before scaling.

cards.title: Design trials to overcome non-use, not just purchase risk
cards.summary: A no-obligation trial needs a defined evaluation window, easy return terms, and activation reminders so customers actually use the product before deciding.
cards.use_when: Creating a try-before-you-buy, subscription trial, product-rental, or introductory-use offer for an ecommerce product whose value becomes clear through use.
steps: Define the offer precisely: what is included, the evaluation period, what the shopper pays upfront if anything, the return process, return-shipping responsibility, and the purchase or billing event at the end of the period.

For consumable or digital products, consider free usage units rather than describing the value only as a cash discount. The source cites a historical test in which “free minutes” outpulled an equivalent-dollar service discount; test whether a product-use framing works better for your store.
Plan activation before launch. Send reminders and usage guidance during the evaluation period: delivery confirmation, setup instructions, a first-use prompt, and a decision-date reminder.

Where appropriate, offer a time-bound incentive for customers who complete the trial and purchase within the stated window. This is intended to counter trial inertia, not to hide terms or pressure an uninformed buyer.
Measure trial activation, return rate, conversion to purchase, support cost, and margin—not only trial signups.
caveats: The free-unit versus cash-discount result is a single historical example and should be tested in the merchant’s own category.
A longer or easier trial can increase returns, support burden, and inventory exposure; the source does not quantify those trade-offs.

cards.title: Use a loss leader only with a credible back-end plan
cards.summary: A low- or no-margin first purchase can acquire customers, but it works only when the product is genuinely valuable and follow-on economics support the acquisition cost.
cards.use_when: Pricing an entry product, starter kit, paid sample, or affiliate offer intended to acquire new ecommerce customers rather than generate first-order profit.
steps: Choose an entry product with broad category appeal and enough standalone value that customers view the store as worth returning to. Do not use a low-quality item solely to collect contacts.

Calculate the complete first-order economics: product cost, pick-pack cost, shipping subsidy, payment fees, discounts, affiliate commission, refunds, and customer service. If the front-end is unprofitable, explicitly cap the loss you can fund.

If affiliates are part of the strategy, make the commission compelling enough to earn promotion, while recognizing that a 100% commission means the merchant retains no first-sale revenue. The source’s example used this structure to acquire the buyer list, not to profit on the entry sale.
Build the back-end before traffic arrives: relevant post-purchase cross-sells, replenishment reminders, bundles, subscription options, and email flows that extend from the entry product.
Evaluate the program on contribution margin and repeat purchase from the acquired cohort, not on first-order revenue alone.
caveats: The source’s coin and information-product examples are illustrations, not forecasts for physical-product stores.
A loss leader fails if later offers are irrelevant, if repeat purchase is weak, or if cash flow cannot support acquisition and fulfillment before payback.

cards.title: Give an unusually strong offer headline-level prominence
cards.summary: Place standard offers near the conversion point, but feature a genuinely exceptional offer in the headline or above the fold when it resolves the shopper’s main hesitation.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether a promotion, PDP, category page, paid-ad landing page, or email should lead with the offer or with the product’s primary benefit.
steps: Always make the operative offer easy to find at the decision point: beside the add-to-cart control, in cart, on the product page, and in the relevant email or landing-page close.
For a familiar offer, keep the main headline focused on the product outcome or shopper problem, then present the offer prominently as the shopper approaches purchase.

Elevate the offer into the headline or hero area only when it is unusually compelling and directly answers a major objection—for example, an exceptional guarantee attached to an otherwise bold performance claim, or a materially distinctive bundle.

Keep the offer wording concrete. The source contrasts a tangible “free information kit” with vague language such as “send for more information”; ecommerce equivalents should name the exact bonus, quantity, eligibility, and deadline.
Test an offer-led hero against a benefit-led hero rather than assuming that a generous promotion should always dominate the page.
caveats: The source treats offer-led headlines as an exception, not a default.
A strong offer can distract from product differentiation or attract promotion-only buyers; assess margin and post-purchase behavior.

cards.title: Focus ecommerce copy work on the high-leverage decision points
cards.summary: Prioritize the hero message, central positioning, and offer language over minor stylistic edits when improving a product or campaign page.
cards.use_when: Allocating copywriting and design-review time for a PDP, collection page, landing page, email, or checkout promotion.
steps: Audit the first decision sequence: paid-ad or email promise, landing-page hero, product title, main headline, first supporting paragraph, primary visual caption, and add-to-cart area. These are the ecommerce equivalents of the source’s position-dependent copy hot spots.

Clarify the big idea—the specific reason this product matters now and how it differs from alternatives. Do not settle for generic category claims when a sharper positioning angle can frame the same product around a concrete shopper outcome.

Rewrite the offer at the conversion point so it states what is received and under what condition. Changes matter most when they alter the actual proposition, such as price, bundle contents, bonus, delivery threshold, or guarantee period.
Use lower-priority editing for accuracy, compliance, readability, and brand standards, but do not let punctuation-level debate consume the time needed to test the hero, positioning, and offer.
For email, treat the subject line and first paragraph as the equivalent high-leverage entry points; carry the same promise through to the destination page.
caveats: The source’s view that minor edits rarely move response is an opinion; regulated, technical, accessibility-sensitive, and brand-critical copy still requires careful review.
Hot spots differ by traffic source and template, so map the actual shopper journey before revising.

cards.title: Reduce checkout friction while preserving attribution
cards.summary: Make ecommerce forms short and usable, show critical terms and bonuses clearly, and use campaign-specific tracking to identify the offer and creative that produced each order.
cards.use_when: Auditing checkout, a lead-capture form, or a campaign landing page that is losing shoppers before they submit or buy.
steps: Ask only for fields needed to complete the current action. For email capture, usually request name and email only unless another field is required to deliver the promised asset. Add company or phone only when the purchase workflow genuinely needs it.

Treat every extra field as a potential abandonment point. The source cites a report estimating about 20% form abandonment per additional question; use that as a prompt to test field reduction, not as a guaranteed rate.
Display the premium or bonus visually and state the guarantee in legible, nearby copy so shoppers do not need to hunt for the value or risk-reversal terms.
Prevent avoidable payment failures by telling shoppers that the billing name and address must match the payment method where address verification is used. Keep error messages specific and actionable.

Use unique URLs, UTMs, promotion codes, or equivalent current analytics tooling for each campaign variation. Verify the current interfaces and attribution rules in your commerce and analytics platforms before launch.
Test button and page colors in context rather than relying on convention; the source reports one test where subdued ochre beat red, underscoring that color is not universal.
caveats: The source’s abandonment-per-field figure and button-color result come from third-party or single-test observations, not universal ecommerce benchmarks.
Do not remove fields required for fraud prevention, legal compliance, fulfillment, or a clearly disclosed financing flow.

cards.title: Test offer variables with message-matched landing pages
cards.summary: Use controlled A/B tests to choose among offers, prices, headlines, bonuses, guarantees, and page treatments, while keeping the acquisition message consistent with the destination page.
cards.use_when: Choosing between competing ecommerce promotions or diagnosing a landing page, PDP, or acquisition campaign with weak conversion.
steps: Write a test hypothesis around one meaningful variable: offer framing, price, bundle, bonus, guarantee, hero headline, visual, or lead. Avoid changing several major elements if the goal is to learn which one caused the outcome.
Split comparable traffic or customer segments between variants. Give each paid ad, email, affiliate placement, or offline creative a distinct tracked destination or campaign identifier.

Match the acquisition promise to the landing-page headline and primary offer. A shopper who clicked an ad for a specific bundle, benefit, or promotion should immediately see that same proposition on arrival.

Measure the relevant ecommerce outcome: completed purchases and contribution margin for purchase campaigns; qualified email captures and later purchase rate for lead campaigns. Do not confuse lead conversion with checkout conversion.
Continue iterating rather than declaring the product unsuccessful after one weak page. The source recommends testing headlines, visuals, prices, bonuses, guarantees, subheads, and leads.
Expect some losing tests. The source argues that merchants should use statistically valid splits rather than settle offer disputes by internal preference.
caveats: The source’s examples of large test gains and its estimate of a low new-promotion success rate are illustrative, not predictions.
A clean read needs sufficient sample size, stable tracking, comparable traffic, and a preselected success metric; do not overreact to small differences.

cards.title: Build a risk-reversing offer with a tested guarantee and deadline
cards.summary: Combine a clear related premium, an understandable guarantee, and legitimate urgency to make the purchase feel safer and more timely, then test the terms against margin and returns.
cards.use_when: Creating or auditing a product-launch, seasonal, bundle, cart, or checkout offer where shoppers hesitate over risk, timing, or value.
steps: Put the risk reversal in plain language: what the customer may return, by when, in what condition, how the refund works, and who pays return shipping. Make the policy easy to find on the PDP, cart, and checkout rather than burying it.
The source recommends unconditional guarantees of at least 60 days and preferably 90 days. Treat that as a testable starting position for eligible products, not a mandatory standard.
Pair the guarantee with a concrete premium when it reinforces product use or perceived value—for example, a relevant guide, accessory, sample, or complementary item.

Create urgency only through a real deadline or limited condition: a stated promotional end date, a seasonal delivery cutoff, a limited bundle, or a genuinely constrained inventory allocation. Ensure ads, email, PDPs, cart, and checkout all show consistent terms.
Test price and terms rather than assuming the lowest price will win. Compare variants on conversion, average order value, refund rate, support cost, and contribution margin.
caveats: The source claims offers can create very large response lifts, but that range is not a promise for a particular store.
Longer unconditional guarantees may increase refund rates, reverse-logistics costs, or abuse; exclude products where hygiene, customization, perishability, or law makes the policy unsuitable.

input.source_name: How to Create Irresistible Offers The Easiest Way on Earth to Make Your Marketing Generate More Leads, Orders, and Sales (1).docx

cards.title: B2B premiums: tie the gift to the buyer's company, not personal use
cards.summary: In corporate B2B marketing, a discount or company-relevant premium beats a personal-use gift because the buyer is rewarded for being a sharp buyer.
cards.use_when: Designing a bonus or premium for a business buyer, especially a corporate employee who must justify the purchase to management
steps: Recognize the incentive asymmetry: a corporate buyer looks good to management by getting the lowest price, so a larger discount may outperform a free gift intended for personal use.
If you do offer a premium to a business buyer, make it related to the product and valuable to the buyer's company — not to the buyer personally.

Model it on the publisher of high-priced technical journals on CD-ROM that offered a free CD-ROM stacker and reader with a group purchase: high perceived value, tightly tied to the product, and it made the prospect look like a smart buyer.
For lead generation specifically, keep the premium directly related to the product or service. Unrelated high-value premiums bring in freebie seekers and unqualified leads.
Modest premiums directly related to the product or service increase total response and still bring a greater volume of qualified leads, even though some serial freebie seekers will always respond.
caveats: The source's preference for related premiums is stated as personal experience, not a universal law; unrelated high-value premiums can still generate volume if raw lead count is the goal.
A discount-only strategy may train buyers to wait for discounts and can erode margin.

cards.title: Use the premium as a gate for a salesperson visit (Ricoh pattern)
cards.summary: A free report or gift can be conditioned on accepting a demonstration, letting the premium qualify and pull prospects into the sales process.
cards.use_when: Planning a lead-generation campaign where a sales rep must get in front of the prospect before a sale can happen
steps: Lead with a soft offer such as 'send for the free report,' which the source says is the most common use of a related premium.
Tie the premium to a harder next step when you need a meeting: offer the impressive report on the condition that a salesperson hand-delivers it.

Follow the Ricoh model: the mailing offered a small gift as an incentive to reply, then Ricoh called to schedule a demonstration; the gift was delivered personally by the rep only after the demonstration.
This conditions the giveaway on the prospect's time and interest, which filters out pure freebie seekers while still lifting reply rates.
Apply the same structure to ecommerce by gating a high-value guide or sample kit behind a scheduled consultation, demo, or onboarding call when the product needs explanation.
caveats: The gate reduces total responses by design; you are trading volume for qualification.
Delivery must actually happen as promised — a delayed or missing gift damages trust at the worst moment in the sales process.

cards.title: Sample offers: let prospects test your product or service on their own material
cards.summary: A sample offer renders the service or runs the product on the prospect's own input so they can judge fit before buying.
cards.use_when: Selling equipment, software, or a technical service where the buyer must see results on their own data before committing
steps: Frame the offer as rendering the service or letting the customer use the product on a sample basis, either to demonstrate capability or to analyze needs.

Use a concrete customer-supplied input. The pelletizer manufacturer asked prospects to send a five-pound bag of their compound with the desired pellet size; the company ran it and returned the pellets to show quality.
Graver Chemical used the same logic for Ecosorb filtration medium: 'Is Ecosorb right for your application? We'd be delighted to evaluate a water sample.'

For software, demonstrate live on the prospect's problem. When a skeptical buyer asked how long a custom database application would take, the rep built a working prototype against their database in 30 minutes instead of answering — the prospect bought on the spot.
Adapt for ecommerce: offer a free audit, a sample sized to the customer's spec, or a same-day configured demo on their data rather than a generic trial.
caveats: Sample programs carry fulfillment cost and turnaround time; set expectations for how fast you return results.
The source's examples are B2B and service settings — transfer the structure, not the unverified claim that it works identically for consumer ecommerce.

cards.title: Trial and evaluation offers: no-cost use for a set period, no obligation
cards.summary: Let prospects use the product or service free for a specified window with the option to return at your expense or buy at list price.
cards.use_when: Designing a trial for physical equipment, software, or a metered service where usage itself demonstrates value
steps: Define the trial precisely: a specified period, no cost, no obligation to buy. The pelletizer maker shipped the machine for a month at no obligation, then let the prospect return it at the manufacturer's expense or buy it.
For metered services, translate the trial into free usage units: an online database or long-distance service can offer '30 minutes of use free.'

Note the measured framing effect from Jim Kobs' book on two MCI ads: '30 free minutes' of long-distance pulled roughly twice the response of '$5 off' the phone bill because the minutes were perceived as greater value — even though both discount the service.
For product evaluations, phrase it as shipping at no cost for whatever technical evaluation the buyer needs, with the option to return and owe nothing or buy at list price.

Combat trial inertia — prospects who request the product and then never open it — by bundling the trial with a decision incentive: 'If you accept the free trial and buy within 30 days, take 10 percent off.'
Send periodic reminders by mail or phone during the evaluation window to get more prospects to actually try the product and lift lead-to-sale conversion.
caveats: Free trials and evaluations fail through inertia, laziness, or lack of time, not necessarily lack of interest — plan the nudge sequence before launch.
The MCI comparison is a single historical test; verify whether free-unit framing beats a cash discount in your own market with a split test.

cards.title: Loss leaders online: fund a cheap front-end with full affiliate commission
cards.summary: Sell a genuinely valuable product at near or below cost to build a customer list, and use attractive affiliate economics to drive the volume.
cards.use_when: Launching an online information product where the strategic goal is acquiring a large customer list rather than per-unit profit
steps: Create the loss leader as a product with wide appeal across your market, valuable enough that buyers will return to you for more. The source's example is an e-book priced at a $39 list.
Approach affiliates — online marketers you have a commission agreement with — and propose they sell the $39 e-book to their lists at $19, framed as a $20 discount.

Instead of the customary 50 percent commission, offer affiliates 100 percent of the $19 sale. Rationale: 50 percent of $19 is only $9.50, too little to interest them, while 100 percent of $19 equals a 50 percent commission on a $38 sale and gets their attention.
Set the $39 list price so the math works: a $20 customer discount and a $19 affiliate payout both look strong, leaving you the list.

Profit comes afterward by selling the newly acquired customers additional products at regular mark-up, the same pattern coin dealers used by selling an American Silver Eagle at 'our cost' and then pitching a $200 set.
caveats: The coin-dealer numbers (10,000 first orders producing 1,000 sets and $200,000) are an example, not a forecast.
You must give real value at the loss-leader price or customers will not return; the strategy depends on back-end offer quality.
Paying 100 percent commission means the first sale produces no revenue for you — model cash flow accordingly.

cards.title: Place the offer in the copy according to its strength
cards.summary: Strong-but-standard offers belong in the close; unusually generous offers deserve outer-envelope or headline prominence.
cards.use_when: Deciding where in a mailing, ad, or landing page to feature the offer
steps: Always feature the offer prominently on the response device — reply card, order form, or checkout element.
For a strong but standard offer, describe it in the closing section of the promotion, and mention it elsewhere in the copy as appropriate.

The more compelling or unusual the offer, the more prominently feature it. McGraw-Hill's Chemical Engineer's Book Club put an unusually generous free copy of Perry's Handbook on the outer envelope with the teaser asking why they were giving away the 50th Anniversary Edition practically for free.

Leading with the offer in a headline is the exception, not the default — but do it when the offer is particularly powerful, as in 'Develop applications up to 6X faster — guaranteed or your money back,' where the guarantee in the headline answers skepticism about a big promise up front.
In the source's own letter promoting copywriting services, the free Mini-Report is the lead, which generated a 3 percent response on a mailing to a couple hundred newsletter publishers.
caveats: Response figures cited are from the source's own campaigns and its clients' testimonials; treat them as examples, not benchmarks.
An offer-led headline trades product or prospect focus for offer focus — test whether it fits your audience.

cards.title: Focus copywriting effort on the three hot spots
cards.summary: Most copy edits are irrelevant to response; only the positioning-dependent lead sections, the big idea, and the offer copy on the reply element materially move results.
cards.use_when: Allocating limited copywriting and review time across a promotion
steps: Spend little time agonizing over punctuation, grammar, spelling, and minor word choice — the source argues these rarely change response between version A and version B.

Hot spot 1, position-dependent copy: in a #10 direct-mail package the outer envelope teaser plus the sales letter headline and lead; in a magalog the front cover, inside front cover, headline and lead, and back cover; on a landing page the banner, headline, salutation, and lead; in email the subject line and first paragraph.

Hot spot 2, the central message or big idea — how you position the selling proposition. For an energy-stock newsletter, that is the difference between hedging a portfolio against an oil-triggered bear market versus profiting from crude reaching $200 a barrel.

Hot spot 3, the offer copy on the reply element — how the offer itself is expressed. 'Free information kit' usually generates more leads than the vaguer 'send for more information' because a kit feels more tangible and valuable.
On an order form, a single word change matters only when it changes the offer: '$100 a year' versus '$500 a year,' or a 10-day versus 90-day money-back guarantee.
Keep polishing headlines, leads, offer copy, theme, and big idea until you are confident they can work.
caveats: The claim that most copy edits are inconsequential is the source's opinion; regulated, technical, or brand-sensitive copy may still require strict editing.
Hot-spot positions differ by format — map them to your actual channel before rewriting.

cards.title: Reply cards still lift total response, even online
cards.summary: Enclosing a physical reply device signals that a reply is expected and raises response across mail, phone, and web channels.
cards.use_when: Producing a lead-generation or order mailing while worrying that prospects will only respond online or by phone
steps: Keep the reply card in the mailing even if most prospects will not use it — the source disagrees with marketers who omit it in the internet age.
Reason: the card graphically signals that the prospect is supposed to reply, and it lifts total response including phone and online responses, not just mail.

For a lead-generating direct mail, the simplest card has the prospect check which offers they want, fill in contact details, and return it — postage can be required from the prospect or prepaid via business reply.

Add a perforated tear-off stub to the reply card to spotlight the premium with a picture, or let the prospect keep it as an order record with space for date and check number; it can also highlight the guarantee.

For space ads, include a reply coupon in the bottom right corner and specify a right-hand page in the insertion order so it is easy to clip. The source reports this increases response by roughly 10 to 15 percent based on personal experience.
Offer multiple response channels — mail, fax, web, email, and a toll-free phone number — rather than assuming phone or web is preferred.
caveats: The 10–15 percent coupon lift is the author's experience, not a tested benchmark for your audience.
Print-ad coupons are now uncommon; the effect may differ in current media environments.

cards.title: Order device formats: order card, BRE, 8.5x11 form, invoice style
cards.summary: Choose an order device format based on how much selling copy you need and how payment returns.
cards.use_when: Designing the order form or reply element for a direct-mail or mail-order promotion
steps: For an order-generating package, use an order card or form plus a #9 business reply envelope so the recipient can return the order with payment.

The classic reply element in a #10 package was a 4 x 9 inch order card that fit in the BRE without folding; many marketers now use an 8 1/2 x 11 inch order form that folds like a letter for the BRE because it holds more copy.

Try the invoice-style order form: list every feature or benefit as a separate 'item' with a price or value, creating the perception that the prospect is getting a lot for the money. The source notes it is widely used for newsletter and magazine subscriptions, with Kiplinger's as an example.
Note the disagreement on clutter: some marketers swear a busier, more cluttered order form pulls better, while others prefer clean, easy-to-fill forms. Test rather than assume.
For membership, mortgage, insurance, and other applications where qualification matters, design the reply element to look like a membership application or official enrollment form.
caveats: Format preferences are practitioner opinions; the source presents both sides and does not declare a winner.
Larger order forms cost more to print and mail — weigh against expected lift.

cards.title: Stickers, tokens, and the yes/no/maybe offer on the reply device
cards.summary: Physical interactive elements on order forms are a proven response booster, and the yes/no/maybe offer lets undecided prospects reply without committing.
cards.use_when: Adding engagement mechanics to a direct-mail order form or considering a softer response option for hesitant prospects
steps: Use tokens, peel-off stickers, stamp sheets, and similar physical devices on the order form — the source calls them proven response boosters and often neglected.
For multiple products such as magazine subscriptions, print a stamp sheet with each magazine's name and picture; the customer affixes stamps for the titles they want.

Build a yes/no/maybe offer with or without stickers: 'yes' affixes to the order sheet to buy, 'maybe' requests a free trial for the less certain, and 'no' selects the negative offer described elsewhere in the source.
Simpler variants use only yes/no stickers, or just a yes sticker.
The value is that hesitation has a place to go — a 'maybe' reply still captures the prospect and a lead rather than losing them entirely.
caveats: These mechanics assume a physical mail piece; online equivalents require different design.
The source gives no measured lift figures for stickers, only that they are established practice.

cards.title: Nine techniques for response-maximizing order devices
cards.summary: Concrete design moves — premium images, prominent guarantees, roomy forms, key codes, short web forms, AVS copy, and color — that raise reply and order rates.
cards.use_when: Reviewing a reply element or online order form before production or launch
steps: Show a picture of the premium: a photo of merchandise, the front cover of a free special report, or multiple report covers fanned out.
Highlight the guarantee on the order device with a certificate-style border, the owner's signature beneath the copy, and clear legible type.
Leave enough space for name and address; cramped areas cause prospects to give up in frustration.
If you key-code via the mailing label, design the piece so the label returns with the response device — affix or imprint the label on the reply element.

Track phone responses without a unique number per promotion by putting 'Ask for Betty' or 'Ask for Extension 112' after the number and having operators ask callers which extension they want; for web traffic, send each promotion to a unique URL.
Create short, memorable, product-connected domain names like myveryfirstebook.com or beer.com, which get more traffic than long names without a logical connection.

On web lead forms, ask the minimum qualifying questions. DM News (10/20/08) reported roughly 20 percent of visitors abandon the form per field or question presented; consumer forms usually need only name and email, B2B may add company and phone, and if the sales process requires an inbound call, phone is mandatory.
For ecommerce order pages, add copy reminding the customer that the name entered must match the name on the credit card exactly, to reduce AVS mismatches and rejected-card complaints.

Test color rather than assuming: in one test, subdued ochre order buttons beat red by 27 percent; in direct mail, print the order card on stock in a different color from the outer envelope and letter — canary yellow and robin's egg blue are favorites.
caveats: The 20 percent abandonment-per-field figure and the 27 percent button-color result come from cited third-party and single-test sources; re-verify against your own traffic.
Color preferences are context-dependent — the source calls the ochre-over-red result surprising.

cards.title: Expect losing tests and run more of them
cards.summary: Even the best baseball team loses four in ten games; direct marketers should expect under-performance and test often enough to find winners.
cards.use_when: Setting expectations for a testing program or deciding whether to abandon direct marketing after a failed campaign
steps: Accept the source's baseball analogy: the best record in Major League Baseball still lost four of every ten games, so a percentage of test campaigns under-performing the control or losing money is normal.
Experienced direct marketers accept this because finding one winner in every two, three, or even five tests can be highly profitable.
Avoid the small-business trap of testing once every few years and then declaring that direct marketing does not work if the first attempt fails.
Do more testing of offers, reply elements, copy, and prices than you currently do.

Quantify the cost of not testing: a single promotion for a new product has roughly a 10 percent success rate in the source's framing, so a one-shot launch is about 10-to-1 against you; a .250 hitter with one at-bat has only a one in four chance of getting on base.
Put propositions to a statistically valid A/B split rather than settling them by judgment around a conference table.
caveats: The 10 percent launch-success rate is the author's estimate, not a measured industry constant.
Volume testing requires enough list or traffic size for a valid split.

cards.title: Run offer A/B splits and match landing page to ad
cards.summary: Split traffic between two offers or headlines with separate URLs, keep the landing page headline consistent with the ad, and let data pick the winner.
cards.use_when: Choosing between two offers, headlines, prices, or page variants when you cannot decide subjectively
steps: If you are mailing 5,000 postcards and cannot choose between two headlines, split the mailing in half rather than picking one — choosing subjectively gives a 50 percent chance of selecting the wrong appeal.
Drive each version to a different URL so you can measure click-through and conversion rates and see which generates the most leads.
Match the landing page headline to the ad headline, especially on the web, so the prospect knows they arrived in the right place.
When a landing page converts poorly, do not abandon the product — test different headlines, visuals, pricing, bonuses, guarantees, subheads, and copy leads, then fold the winners into the page.
Follow Peter Betuel's principle in the source: what matters is not what you think, like, believe, or prefer but what your prospects think, like, believe, and prefer.

Expect surprises. A car-rental-by-the-week company tested a free upgrade (A) against a rental discount tied to buying multiple weeks in advance with a book of tickets (B); offer B won by a wide margin with nearly a tenfold revenue increase.
caveats: The rental-company result is one case study, not a prediction for your offer.
Clean A/B reads require enough traffic or list size per cell and one changed variable at a time.

cards.title: Match the promo headline to the landing page for split tests
cards.summary: When testing headlines via ads or postcards, carry the same headline onto the landing page and use a unique URL per version for clean measurement.
cards.use_when: Running a split test across an ad, postcard, or email that sends traffic to a landing page
steps: Split the traffic source itself, not just the destination — half the postcards carry 'Tastes Great,' half carry 'Less Filling.'
Give each version its own URL so click-through and conversion rates can be attributed correctly.
Ensure the landing page headline matches the headline used in the ad or postcard that produced the click.
Then watch which version pulls slightly better and begin incorporating the winning elements into the page.
On the web this is fast and inexpensive relative to offline testing, which is why the source recommends iterating landing pages rather than giving up on a poorly converting product.
caveats: Mismatched headline and page is called out by the source as a specific risk in this type of test.
Small samples can produce noise — do not act on a slight difference without enough volume.

cards.title: Premium and guarantee offer summary: what to default to and how to test it
cards.summary: The source's closing synthesis: word and present offers prominently, expect 10–900 percent response lifts, and default to related premiums, 60–90 day unconditional guarantees, and urgency.
cards.use_when: Building or auditing a complete offer: premium, guarantee, urgency, and risk reversal
steps: Treat wording and presentation as tremendously important — the right offer can boost response rates by 10 to 900 percent according to the source, and stressing the offer in copy generates more leads and orders.
Use a premium (a free gift with order or inquiry) as the easiest way to increase response, and favor free information such as a special report, CD, or video.
Make guarantees at least 60 days and preferably 90 days, and keep them unconditional — return the product, get your money back.
Create urgency by giving the prospect a deadline or other incentive to respond now rather than later.
Design the offer so all the risk sits on the seller rather than the buyer; make buying entirely risk-free.
Test prices and terms rather than intuiting them — the source reports that the lower price is frequently not the winner.
Accept that no one can predict which offer will respond best; only a series of A/B split tests will find the winning offer for your product or service.
caveats: The 10–900 percent range is the author's broad experience claim, not a guaranteed outcome.
Longer unconditional guarantees can raise refund rates — the source does not address this trade-off.
The preference for 90 days over shorter terms is the source's recommendation; test it against your margin and return behavior.

cards.title: Use a related premium as the easy default for lead generation
cards.summary: Free booklets, reports, and product-related gifts raise response volume while attracting more qualified leads than unrelated high-value giveaways.
cards.use_when: Choosing a lead magnet or inquiry incentive for a campaign
steps: Default to a free booklet or report related to the product or service — the source says this is his personal favorite and is most often used in a soft offer ('Send for free report').

Expect modest, directly related premiums to increase total responses and deliver a greater volume of qualified leads from good prospects, even though serial freebie seekers will always respond to anything free.
Avoid unrelated high-value premiums in lead generation because they bring in large numbers of freebie seekers and other unqualified leads.
You can tie the free report to a harder next step, as when a report is promised only if a salesperson hand-delivers it — which converts a soft offer into a qualified appointment.
Remember the B2B adjustment: if the buyer is a corporate employee, a discount or company-relevant premium may outperform a personal-use gift.
caveats: The preference for related premiums is stated as the author's experience, not a tested rule.
Some freebie responses are unavoidable and should be planned for in lead-scoring and follow-up.
